title: Observability in Python: structlog, contextvars, prometheus_client and profiling
seriesDescription: Prometheus and tracing, JWT and FastAPI auth, pytest and mocks. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Correlation ids with ContextVar and structlog, prometheus_client metrics and multiprocess mode, OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation, and finding slow code with py-spy and cProfile.
source: Python documentation (contextvars, logging, cProfile); structlog documentation (contextvars); prometheus_client documentation (metric types, multiprocess mode); OpenTelemetry Python documentation; py-spy README

questions.prompt: In a FastAPI app, write a `ContextVar` named `request_id` and an HTTP middleware that sets it from the `x-request-id` header (or a new `uuid4` string) for the duration of the request and resets it afterwards.
questions.starter:
from contextvars import ContextVar
from uuid import uuid4

checks.label: reads the header or makes a uuid4

questions.explanation: `ContextVar` values follow asyncio tasks, unlike `threading.local`, so every log call in the request can read `request_id.get()` from a `logging.Filter`. Using `structlog.contextvars.bind_contextvars` is an equally good answer.

questions.prompt: Write a `logging.Filter` subclass named `RequestIdFilter` whose `filter` method copies `request_id.get()` onto `record.request_id` and lets every record through.
questions.explanation: Attach it to a handler (`handler.addFilter(RequestIdFilter())`) and reference `%(request_id)s` in the format string. Filters on a handler run for every record that handler emits, including records from other loggers.

questions.prompt: Configure structlog so that values bound with `structlog.contextvars` appear in every event and events are rendered as JSON, then bind `request_id="r-1"` for the current context.
questions.explanation: Verified with structlog: a later `log.info("hello", x=1)` prints `{"x": 1, "event": "hello", "request_id": "r-1"}`. Call `clear_contextvars()` at the start of each request so values never leak between requests.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A `ContextVar` set inside one asyncio request task is not visible to another request task running at the same time.
questions.reason: Each asyncio task runs in its own copy of the context taken when the task was created.

whys.a: Correct: Task-local copies isolate the values, which is why ContextVar works for per-request data in async code.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: A task created with `asyncio.create_task` copies the context at creation, so it sees the parent value set earlier but its own later changes stay private.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: `ContextVar.reset(token)` restores the value the variable had before the matching `set()` call.
questions.reason: The contextvars module was added to the standard library in Python 3.7.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: Both are true, but the module's release version does not explain how reset works; the token records the previous value.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Always reset in a finally block so an exception cannot leave a stale value behind.

questions.prompt: With `prometheus_client`, define a `Counter` `http_requests_total` with labels `method` and `status` and a `Histogram` `http_request_seconds`, then record one GET that returned 200 taking the time of `handle()`.
questions.model:
REQS = Counter("http_requests_total", "Requests", ["method", "status"])
LAT = Histogram("http_request_seconds", "Latency")
REQS.labels("GET", "200").inc()
with LAT.time():
    handle()
questions.explanation: Labels must come from a small closed set. `observe(seconds)` is the explicit alternative to the timer context manager.

questions.prompt: Match each `prometheus_client` metric class with what it records.

right.text: A total that only increases and resets on restart
A value that can go up and down, such as in-flight requests
Observations counted into buckets so percentiles can be estimated
A running count and sum of observations
A free-text event with a timestamp

questions.explanation: The Python `Summary` exposes only `_count` and `_sum`, with no quantiles, so use a `Histogram` when you need percentiles across instances.

questions.prompt: Which series name does `prometheus_client` expose for `Counter("jobs_done", "Jobs finished")` after one `inc()`?

options.why: The bare name is used for gauges, not counters.
The `_count` suffix belongs to histograms and summaries.
Correct: the client appends `_total` to counter names (checked against `prometheus_client` 0.26).

questions.explanation: A `jobs_done_created` series with the creation timestamp is exported too. Name counters without the suffix in code, query them with it in PromQL.

questions.prompt: `prometheus_client`'s `Histogram` uses 14 default finite bucket boundaries from 0.005 to 10 seconds. How many `le` bucket series does one `Histogram` expose per label combination, including `+Inf`?
questions.explanation: The 14 finite boundaries plus the cumulative `+Inf` bucket give 15 (checked by exposing a histogram with the default buckets). Choose buckets around your SLO threshold instead of keeping the defaults when latency targets are far from them.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: With four uvicorn worker processes and default `prometheus_client` settings, one scrape returns the combined totals of all four workers.
questions.reason: Each worker process keeps its metrics in its own memory, so a scrape sees only the worker that answers it.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Correct: A is false: each scrape reflects one worker only. R is true and is the cause.

questions.explanation: Use multiprocess mode (the `PROMETHEUS_MULTIPROC_DIR` environment variable and `MultiProcessCollector`) or one process per container so scrapes see complete data.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: In a `prometheus_client` `Histogram` the bucket `le="1.0"` also counts observations of 0.3 seconds.
questions.reason: Bucket counters are reset to zero each time Prometheus scrapes them.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is true because buckets are cumulative. R is false: counters keep growing until the process restarts.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: The cumulative design is what makes buckets additive across instances and what `histogram_quantile` relies on.

questions.prompt: Write the shell command that starts the ASGI app `main:app` with uvicorn under OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation, naming the service `orders` through the `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` environment variable.
questions.explanation: Install `opentelemetry-distro` and run `opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install` to add instrumentation packages for the libraries in use. The `--service_name` option is an equivalent way to set the name. Do not combine auto-instrumentation with the uvicorn `--reload` option.

questions.prompt: Write the shell command that records a 30 second flame graph of the running Python process 4321 to `flame.svg` with `py-spy`, without restarting it.
questions.explanation: `py-spy` is a sampling profiler that reads the process memory, so it needs ptrace permission (often root). `py-spy dump --pid` prints the current stacks, like a thread dump.

questions.prompt: Write Python that profiles a call to `handle()` with `cProfile` and prints the results sorted by cumulative time.
questions.explanation: `pstats.Stats(profile).sort_stats("cumulative").print_stats(20)` also works. `cProfile` traces every call, so overhead is higher than `py-spy` sampling; use it in development or on a copy of the workload.

questions.prompt: An async FastAPI handler calls the blocking `requests.get()` directly. Under load p99 climbs while CPU stays low, and `py-spy dump` shows the main thread inside a socket read. What is happening?

options.text: The garbage collector pauses every request for as long as the socket read lasts.
options.why: Garbage collection does not wait on sockets.

options.text: The blocking call stalls the event loop so other requests wait.
options.why: Correct: one thread runs the loop, and a blocking call freezes all coroutines.

options.text: The uvicorn access log is flushed to disk synchronously once for every single request.
options.why: A flush would appear as a write, not a socket read, and is rarely the bottleneck.

options.text: The Prometheus client is holding a global lock and thereby serialising all route handlers.
options.why: Metric updates are short and do not hold sockets.

questions.explanation: Use an async client such as `httpx.AsyncClient`, or run the blocking call in a thread with `asyncio.to_thread` (or declare the route with plain def so FastAPI uses its thread pool).

questions.prompt: True or false: `cProfile` has such low overhead that it is the best choice for always-on profiling of a production service.

options.why: `cProfile` hooks every function call and return, which slows programs noticeably.
Correct: a deterministic profiler adds overhead proportional to call count.

questions.explanation: Prefer a sampling profiler such as `py-spy` for production, and `cProfile` for local runs or a replay of the workload.
